vignette:
Sarah sits across from me, her firefighter’s uniform replaced by a simple grey t-shirt and jeans. Her posture is a contradiction: shoulders squared with disciplined strength, but her hands are clenched so tightly in her lap that her knuckles are white. At 26, she has the clear-eyed, capable look of someone you’d want running into a burning building for you. It’s the look she’s trying to hold onto, but the effort is visible in the subtle tremor in her jaw.

Nine months ago, Sarah was the person she always wanted to be. She describes her life before the incident with a kind of wistful pride. She loved the physicality of her job, the structured chaos of a call, the easy camaraderie at the station house. She was the one who checked the gear, who ran the drills with the rookies, who felt a deep sense of purpose in her own competence. She felt safe in her strength.

The call was a three-alarm fire at a textile warehouse on the industrial side of town. It was a long, grueling fight. Hours in, she and her partner, Mike, were doing a secondary search on the second floor when the world became a roar of twisting metal and crumbling brick. The floor gave way. Mike was thrown clear, but Sarah went down with the debris. She came to in absolute darkness, pinned by a steel support beam across her legs and torso.

For the next four hours, she was entombed. She talks about this time in fragmented, sensory details. The taste of plaster dust in her mouth, so thick she felt like she was choking on it. The crushing, immovable weight on her chest that made every breath a battle. The terrifying silence, punctuated only by the drip of water somewhere nearby and the frantic sound of her own heartbeat. She tried to use her radio, but it was just static. She ran through every protocol, every survival technique she’d ever learned, until all that was left was the primal, suffocating certainty that she would die there, alone in the dark.

When the rescue team finally reached her, the sudden beam of a flashlight felt like a physical blow. The hospital stay was a blur of pain medication and worried faces from her crew. Her physical injuries—a fractured tibia, three broken ribs, and a concussion—were significant, but they were the easy part. They healed.

The real trouble started when she got home. The first time she smelled her neighbor’s barbecue, the scent of smoke sent her to the floor, gasping for air, the weight of the beam phantomly pressing on her chest. She began sleeping with all the lights on, terrified of the darkness. Small spaces became impossible; she once had a full-blown panic attack in the station’s locker room and had to flee, leaving her gear on the floor.

She feels like a ghost haunting her own life. The easy banter with her crew now feels forced and hollow. They look at her with a mixture of pity and concern that feels like a judgment. She sees the doubt in their eyes when they’re gearing up for a call, and worse, she feels it in herself. The woman who once ran into fires without a second thought now hesitates at her own front door. She has snapped at her parents for no reason, pushed away friends who try to ask how she’s doing, and hasn’t been on a date since the accident. The world, which once felt full of purpose and challenge, now feels like a series of potential traps.

She has been cleared for light duty, but she mostly calls in sick. The uniform hangs in her closet, a reminder of a person she no longer recognizes. “They pulled my body out of that building,” she said quietly in our last session, her gaze fixed on a point far beyond my office wall. “But I think they left me in there.”
